[Get started](v01-get-started.html) introduced params with three
examples. This vignette goes deeper: what a param holds, how its rules work,
how params are grouped into configs and set in a pipeline, and how they
appear in a document. It builds on pipeflow's vignettes
[Annotated parameter values](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v05d-param-value.html)
(the hook that pubflow's params use) and
[Pipeline views](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v03b-pipeline-views.html).

```{r library}
library(pipeflow)
library(pubflow)
```

## A param is a value with attributes

A param is a value together with attributes that describe it. The functions
of a pipeline never see the attributes, they get the plain value.

```{r param}
xVar <- choice_param(
    "Temp.Celsius",
    choices = c("Temp.Celsius", "Wind", "Solar.R"),
    label = "Predictor",
    description = "Variable that explains the ozone concentration",
    source = "user"
)
xVar
```

The accessors read the value and the attributes:

```{r accessors}
param_value(xVar)
param_type(xVar)
param_attr(xVar, "label")
```

Base functions work on a param as on its value, so `xVar == "Wind"` and
`levels(xVar)` work as expected. Note that `identical(xVar, "Temp.Celsius")`
is `FALSE`, because the attributes are part of the object. Hand
`param_value()` to code that expects a plain value.

Besides `label` and `description`, pubflow knows the attributes `source`
(e.g. `"user"` for the params that the user sets), `area` (a group of params),
`advanced` (shown in a collapsed block), `locked` (shown as a disabled input,
see [Locked params](#locked-params)) and a few more for the UI. Any other
named argument is stored as well. `?param` lists all of them.

## Constructors and validity

Each constructor comes with a rule that tells whether a value is valid.
`param_validity()` applies it to the param's own value or to any other value
and returns one message per rule, `""` meaning valid:

```{r validity}
param_validity(xVar)
param_validity(xVar, value = "Height")

level <- numeric_param(
    0.95,
    label = "Confidence level",
    min = 0.5,
    max = 0.999,
    source = "user"
)
param_validity(level, value = 1.5)
```

`numeral_param()` is for numbers that must keep their decimal places. A
number like `0.90` is `0.9` as soon as it is a number; a numeral holds the
text and checks that it can be read as a number, in the given bounds:

```{r numeral}
limit <- numeral_param("80.0", label = "Ozone limit (ppb)", min = 0)
param_value(limit)
param_validity(limit, value = "abc")
param_validity(limit, value = "-5")
```

To add a rule of your own, use `add_validity()`. A rule is a function that
takes the plain value and returns `""` or a message. It is used in addition
to the default rule:

```{r add-validity}
level <- add_validity(level, \(x) {
    if (x != 0.5) "" else "a level of 0.5 is not allowed"
})
param_validity(level, value = 0.5)
```

A rule that fails with an error counts as a message too, so a faulty rule
never breaks a parameter UI. Own constructors for recurring kinds of params,
which wrap one of the above, are shown in the examples of `?param`.

## Groups

`param_group()` combines params that belong together, here the range of
temperatures that the analysis uses. The group is shown side by side in a UI
and checked as a whole: each child by its own rule and the group by rules that
see all children. Such a rule is added with `add_validity()` as well:

```{r group}
window <- param_group(
    list(
        from = numeric_param(0, label = "From", min = -20, max = 60),
        to = numeric_param(30, label = "To", min = -20, max = 60)
    ),
    label = "Temperature range (°C)",
    source = "user",
    area = "data"
) |>
    add_validity(\(x) if (x$from < x$to) "" else "'From' must be below 'To'")

param_validity(window)
param_validity(window, value = list(from = 30, to = 10))
```

The result has one element for the group and one per child. A step gets the
value of a group as a plain named list, so `prep` below reads `window$from` and
`window$to`.

## Configs

A *config* collects the params of an analysis. It numbers the params in the
order given (the order of a parameter UI). Combining configs numbers them anew.

```{r config}
base <- param_config(
    xVar = xVar,
    level = level,
    window = window,
    title = param("Ozone in New York", label = "Report title", source = "user")
)
base
```

Configs are combined with `c()`. Names must be unique, unless you say that the
first definition wins. That is useful for a stricter variant of a config, e.g.
for a validated analysis, that overrides single params of the base config:

```{r config-merge}
strict <- param_config(
    level = numeric_param(
        0.99,
        label = "Confidence level",
        min = 0.5,
        max = 0.999,
        source = "user",
        locked = TRUE
    )
)
config <- c(strict, base, .duplicates = "first")
names(config)
param_value(config$level)
```

## Params in a pipeline

The analysis is the pipeline of the Get started vignette with a filter on the
temperature and a table of the coefficients. The functions are written with
plain defaults that equal the values of the config.

The table is made by a function defined outside the pipeline, as in Get
started:

```{r coef-table}
coef_table <- function(model, level) {
    ci <- confint(model, level = level)
    coefs <- data.frame(
        term = rownames(ci),
        estimate = coef(model),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
    pub_table(
        coefs,
        caption = sprintf("Coefficients with %g%% confidence limits", 100 * level),
        labels = c(
            term = "Term",
            estimate = "Estimate",
            lower = "Lower",
            upper = "Upper"
        ),
        digits = c(estimate = 3L, lower = 3L, upper = 3L)
    )
}
```

```{r pipeline}
pip <- pip_new("ozone") |>
    pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) data) |>
    pip_add(
        "prep",
        function(df = ~data, window = list(from = 0, to = 30)) {
            df[, "Temp.Celsius"] <- (df[, "Temp"] - 32) * 5 / 9
            inRange <- df$Temp.Celsius >= window$from & df$Temp.Celsius <= window$to
            df[inRange, ]
        }
    ) |>
    pip_add("fit", function(data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        lm(paste("Ozone ~", xVar), data = data)
    }) |>
    pip_add("coef_table", function(model = ~fit, level = 0.99) {
        coef_table(model, level)
    })
```

The last steps add a summary text, a table of the params (explained in
[A table of parameters](#a-table-of-parameters)) and the layout step:

```{r pipeline-end}
pip |>
    pip_add("summary", function(model = ~fit, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        pub_text(sprintf(
            "**%s** explains %.0f%% of the variance of the ozone concentration.",
            xVar,
            100 * summary(model)$r.squared
        ))
    }) |>
    pip_add(
        "params_table",
        function(
            xVar = "Temp.Celsius",
            level = 0.99,
            window = list(from = 0, to = 30),
            title = "Ozone in New York"
        ) {
            # the arguments are not used: they make the step run again when
            # one of the reported params changes
            pub_params_table(
                pub_get_params(.self, source = "user"),
                caption = "Parameters of the analysis"
            )
        }
    ) |>
    pip_add(
        "report",
        function(
            title = "Ozone in New York",
            summary = ~summary,
            table = ~coef_table,
            params = ~params_table
        ) {
            pub_doc(
                pub_section("Results", summary, table),
                pub_section("Parameters", params),
                title = title
            )
        }
    )
```

`pip_set_params()` sets the params of the config in every step that has an
argument of the same name. A step's plain default has no rules, so this first
application stores the params of the config as they are, without a check. Check
a config before you apply it: `param_validity_assert()` signals an error for an
invalid entry. After that, every new value is checked against the rules of its
param (see below).

```{r check-config}
invisible(lapply(config, param_validity_assert))
```

With `unknown = "error"`, a param that no step has is an error instead of a
warning:

```{r set-params}
pip_set_params(pip, config, unknown = "error")
pip
```

```{r set-unknown, error = TRUE}
pip_set_params(pip, list(alpha = 0.05), unknown = "error")
```

The steps still get plain values. `pub_get_params()` reads the param objects
back. It lists them in the order of the config (`order = "config"`, the
default) or in the order in which the pipeline first uses the names
(`order = "pipeline"`), and it can filter by attributes:

```{r get-params}
names(pub_get_params(pip))
names(pub_get_params(pip, order = "pipeline"))
names(pub_get_params(pip, area = "data"))
```

Setting a value that is not valid is an error, and nothing is set. All
failures are collected into one error that names step and param:

```{r set-invalid, error = TRUE}
pip_set_params(
    pip,
    list(xVar = "Height", window = list(from = 30, to = 10))
)
```

Run the pipeline once. A group is set as a list; this changes the data that
`prep` returns, so `prep` and all steps that depend on it are outdated and run
again:

```{r set-group}
pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
pip_set_params(pip, list(window = list(from = 10, to = 25)))
pip
```

## One value per name

A name has one value in the whole pipeline: `xVar` is the argument of `fit`,
`summary` and `params_table`, and setting it sets all of them. This holds also
if the params are set through a view (e.g. the steps that a parameter UI
shows). pipeflow's
[Pipeline views](https://rpahl.github.io/pipeflow/articles/v03b-pipeline-views.html)
vignette describes this in detail (pipeflow 0.5.0.9027 or later). With
`scope = "view"` only the steps of the view are set:

```{r scope}
xVars <- function(p) {
    sapply(pip_get_params(p, simplify = FALSE)$xVar, as.character)
}

pip_set_params(pip_view(pip, step = "summary"), list(xVar = "Wind"))
xVars(pip)

pip_set_params(
    pip_view(pip, step = "summary"),
    list(xVar = "Solar.R"),
    scope = "view"
)
xVars(pip)
```

Now `summary` explains the ozone concentration with another variable than
`fit`, which is rarely intended. pipeflow warns when a step is added or
replaced with a param that differs from the same param in the other steps:

```{r conflict}
copy <- pip_clone(pip)
pip_add(copy, "note", function(level = 0.9) level)
```

Setting the config again puts the params back. (To change the function of a
step but keep the current values of its params, use the argument `keep_params`
of `pip_replace()`.)

```{r reset}
pip_set_params(pip, config, unknown = "error")
xVars(pip)
```

## A table of parameters

A report documents the params that an analysis used. `pub_params_table()`
makes a table from param objects, by default with their labels, values and
descriptions. Other columns are the name or any attribute:

```{r params-table}
params <- pub_get_params(pip, source = "user")
pub_params_table(params, columns = c(name = "Name", value = "Value", area = "Area")) |>
    pub_cell_text()
```

The step `params_table` above puts the table into the document. It reads the
param objects of the pipeline through `.self`, which a step function can use
without declaring it. The step lists the params it reports as arguments, so
that it runs again when one of them changes. `.self` bypasses the pipeline's
dependency tracking, so list every param that the table reports: one that is
left out can change without the step running again. The layout step takes the
table as an input like any other output:

```{r params-step}
pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
```

```{r html, eval = FALSE}
pub_html(pip[["report", "out"]])
```

```{r html-framed, echo = FALSE}
# The same, framed to set it apart from the vignette's own text, and with
# its headings left out of the table of contents of the pkgdown site
html <- pub_html(pip[["report", "out"]])
htmltools::div(
    style = "border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 0 1em;",
    htmltools::attachDependencies(
        htmltools::HTML(gsub("<h([1-6])", "<h\\1 data-toc-skip", html)),
        htmltools::htmlDependencies(html)
    )
)
```

## Locked params

In a validated analysis, some params are fixed, here the confidence level of
`strict`. A param with `locked = TRUE` is shown in a parameter UI as a
disabled input: the user sees the value but can't change it. The steps run as
usual.

```{r locked}
param_attr(pub_get_params(pip)$level, "locked")
```

The lock binds the UI only. Code can still change a locked param, subject to
its validity rules:

```{r locked-set}
pip_set_params(pip, list(level = 0.9))
param_value(pub_get_params(pip)$level)
```

pipeflow's step locks (`pip_lock()`) are different: a locked step no longer
runs, `pip_set_params()` skips it, and the UI shows its params as locked too. To fix params but keep the
steps running, use the attribute.
